newsitem.title: UK: Foreign military links not seen helping Albania.
newsitem.headline: Foreign military links not seen helping Albania.

text.p: Albania has developed some military ties with the outside world but these are unlikely to be of much use to President Sali Berisha as he struggles to restore order in his country, experts said on Friday.

Albania is a member of NATO's Partnership for Peace, which groups former Soviet allies, and has allowed the United States to use the northern town of Gjader as a base to launch remote-controlled reconnaissance drones over Bosnia.

But Dr Mark Smith of the British Defence Ministry's Conflict Studies Research Centre said Washington's wariness about Albania meant Tirana had little chance of updating its obsolete Soviet-era armed forces.

"The Albanian military would really like to get hold of some decent weapons but they haven't got them as a result of ties with NATO because the Americans have been very careful not to supply them with modern weaponry," he said in a telephone interview.

The American presence peaked between 1992 and 1995, when retired U.S. advisers were frequent visitors to Tirana, but ties deteriorated significantly after parliamentary elections in May 1996 which were widely condemned as flawed.
Berisha faces a popular uprising in the south of Albania by protesters furious at the loss of their life savings in shady pyramid investment schemes.
Several dozen Albanian officers have received training in Germany but Geoffrey Stern from the London School of Economics said the foreign links were largely irrelevant.
"I don't think it's a question of how strong the armed forces are," he said by telephone.
"The army is not reliable -- there is evidence they handed over weapons to the rebels. The army also lost money in these investment schemes."
Smith said that, given the intractable problems facing Albania, it would be hard for foreign military advisers to help reform the country's communist-era armed forces.

"I think that well before the current upheaval an awful lot of U.S. advisers had been replaced by Albanians. They were unlikely to succeed if only because at the end of the day Berisha's commitment to democracy is really only skin deep," he said.

"That makes the process of reforming the military forces extremely difficult," he added, saying some inside the Albanian military had talked about boosting military links with Turkey and possibly even Iran.

Albania was one of the first east European states to express the wish to join NATO but a spokesman for the 16-nation alliance said cooperation was very unlikely to expand beyond the confines of Partnership for Peace.

"It's difficult to imagine any of the 16 members agreeing to invite Albania to start talks on membership. Our cooperation is linked purely to peacekeeping training and does not go beyond that." he said by telephone from Brussels.
Smith rejected the idea that Berisha might turn to foreign mercenaries to help him.
"I would be very surprised if that were the case. If it looks as though the army is turning against Berisha it's possible he would resort to desperate measures," he said.
"I'm not sure where he'd get mercenaries from or how he'd pay them with all the pyramid schemes collapsing."
